title: Reading IPA and the five vowels
sub: How IPA works, and the five pure vowels that are the foundation of a good Spanish accent.

steps.html:
English spelling is unreliable: the letter c is different in "cat" and "city", and ough is different in "though", "through" and "tough".

The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) fixes this. Every symbol stands for exactly one sound, always, in every language. Square brackets mean "this is how it's actually said":
  • "cat" is [kæt] and "city" is [ˈsɪɾi]: two different symbols for the two c's.
  • Spanish casa is [ˈkasa].
Learning IPA alongside Spanish gives you two things: you can read the pronunciation of any word in a dictionary, and you'll notice sounds your ear currently skips over.

Many IPA symbols are ordinary letters and mean roughly what an English speaker expects: [p b t d k m n f s l].

The traps are the symbols that look familiar but mean something else. The most important ones for Spanish:
  • [i] is the "ee" of "see", never the "i" of "sit". So [si] is "see", not "sigh".
  • [e] is "eh", like the start of "say".
  • [a] is "ah"; [u] is "oo".
  • [j] is the y of "yes", never the j of "jam".
  • [x] is a scrapy sound at the back of the mouth (the Spanish jota), never "ks".
Each of these gets its own lesson. For now, just remember: read IPA symbol by symbol, not like English spelling.

steps.html:
Spanish has only five vowel sounds, and their IPA symbols are the same as the letters: [a e i o u]. The catch is that IPA vowels have their "European" values, not their English letter names.

English speakers carry two habits into Spanish vowels:
  1. Gliding. English vowels in "say", "see", "no", "two" move while you say them. Spanish vowels hold perfectly still.
  2. Reducing. English turns unstressed vowels into "uh". Spanish never does.
This lesson fixes gliding on [a], [e] and [i]. The next lesson does [o], [u] and the "uh" habit.

Say English "say" slowly and stretch it: "saaay". Notice that your jaw rises and your tongue moves up toward the end. It isn't one vowel but two: [eɪ].

Now say just the beginning, "seh", and freeze before anything moves. That frozen vowel is Spanish [e]. A mirror helps: during a Spanish vowel your jaw doesn't move at all.
steps.yes: Good. That movement at the end of "say" is the glide [ɪ]. In Spanish, stop before it. Practise "seh, meh, deh" with a still jaw.
steps.no: Put a fingertip lightly under your chin and say "say, day, may" slowly. You should feel your jaw lift a little at the end. Then play the Spanish word and notice it stays put.
steps.q: Did you feel your jaw or tongue move at the end of "say"?

steps.html: Listen for the end of each word. The English one drifts upward; the Spanish one stops dead.

lessons.title: Vowels II: o, u, and no "uh"

steps.html: American "no" is really [noʊ]: the lips keep rounding at the end. Spanish [o] keeps the same lip shape from start to finish.
American English often says "two" with the tongue pushed forward. Spanish [u] is fully back, with tightly rounded lips.

In English, unstressed vowels collapse into a weak "uh" sound. IPA writes it [ə], called schwa. "banana" is [bəˈnænə]: only the middle a is a real a.

Spanish has no schwa at all. Every vowel keeps its full quality whether it's stressed or not. banana is [baˈnana]: three real a's. This one habit is responsible for a big part of an English accent in Spanish.
Compare the unstressed syllables. English blurs them; Spanish doesn't.

If any tap came out as "uh", go slower and exaggerate the vowel.
steps.yes: That's the Spanish rhythm: every syllable gets a beat and a full vowel.
steps.no: Slow right down: one syllable per second, mouth shape clear for each vowel. Speed comes later.

title: Consonants
sub: Every Spanish consonant, one at a time: the ones without a puff, the soft ones, the r's, and the ones you already have.

steps.h: A sound English hides from you
steps.html:
At the start of a stressed syllable, English p, t and k come with a little burst of breath. Phoneticians call it aspiration and write it with a raised h: "pin" is [pʰɪn].

After s, the puff disappears: "spin" is [spɪn]. English speakers never notice, because the difference never changes a word's meaning.

Spanish p, t and k never have the puff, anywhere in a word. The p of English "spin" is exactly the Spanish p.
Hold a tissue, or the back of your hand, a few centimetres from your lips. Say "pin", then "spin". Play the recordings and copy them.
steps.yes: That puff on "pin" is the [ʰ]. Now say "spin" and drop the s, keeping the p exactly as it was: that's Spanish [p].
steps.no: Try a little louder, with the tissue closer. Most people feel a clear puff on "pin" and almost nothing on "spin". You can also try "pot" vs "spot".
steps.q: Did the tissue move for "pin" but not for "spin"?

steps.html: In each pair, listen for the breathy "h" right after the English p.

steps.h: Why Spanish p can sound like b
steps.html:
Your ear uses the puff to tell p from b. Without it, a Spanish [p] can sound like "b" to you, so peso ("weight") and beso ("kiss") seem to blur.

What really separates them is voicing. For [b] your vocal folds are already buzzing while the lips are closed. For [p] they stay silent until the vowel starts.

Put your fingers on your throat. Say "zzzz", then "ssss". The buzz you feel on z is voicing.

Now close your lips and hum, then open them into "ba": the buzz started before the lips opened. Try "pa" the same way: no buzz until the vowel.
steps.yes: Voicing is the key to b vs p, d vs t, and g vs k in Spanish.
steps.no: Press a bit more firmly and make the z long and loud. The buzz is easiest to feel just above the Adam's apple.
steps.q: Did you feel the buzz on "zzzz" but not on "ssss"?

lessons.title: t and d on the teeth

steps.html:
For English t and d, the tip of your tongue touches the gum ridge, the bump just behind your upper teeth. For Spanish t and d, it touches the back of the upper front teeth themselves. Sounds made against the teeth are called dental, and IPA marks them with a little bridge underneath: [t̪ d̪].

Spanish t also follows the no-puff rule from the last lesson. So English "tea" is [tʰi] while Spanish tía starts with [t̪]: further forward, and no breath.

Say English "tea" and notice where your tongue tip lands. Now slide it forward until it presses against the back of your top teeth, and say "ta". Hold a tissue in front of your mouth too: it shouldn't move.
steps.yes: That forward, puff-free t is Spanish [t̪]. Spanish d is made in the same place, with voicing.
steps.no: Say "t" and freeze with the tongue in place. Feel the gum ridge with the tongue tip, then move it a few millimetres forward onto the teeth.
steps.q: Could you feel the difference between the gum ridge and the teeth?

steps.html:
Spanish [k] is written:
  • c before a, o, u: casa, coma, Cuba
  • qu before e, i: queso, quince. The u is silent: it's only there to keep the c hard.
  • k in a few borrowed words: kilo
Like p and t, Spanish k has no puff: think of the k in "skin", not "kin".

Its voiced partner [ɡ] is written g before a, o, u (goma, gato) and gu before e, i (guitarra). IPA uses the round, single-loop ɡ.

steps.h: Spanish has two b's, and no v
steps.html:
First, a surprise: Spanish b and v are the same sound. vaso and baso would sound identical. There's no English-style v (teeth on lip) in Spanish at all.

That one sound comes in two versions:
  • Hard [b]: the lips close completely, like English b.
  • Soft [β]: the lips come close but never touch, and air keeps flowing between them with a light buzz.
The symbol β is the Greek letter beta. Spanish speakers don't think of these as two sounds, so they never mention it, but using a hard [b] between vowels makes your Spanish sound choppy.

Say "aba" with an English b. Now say it again, but don't let your lips touch: leave a tiny gap and keep your voice on, so the air buzzes softly through. It's a bit like blowing gently on hot soup while humming.
steps.yes: That fuzzy, gentle b is [β]. It's what you hear in the middle of lobo and uva.
steps.no: Try looking in a mirror: say "aba" and watch your lips meet. Then repeat while keeping a sliver of light between them. It will feel lazy; that's right.
steps.q: Could you make a b where the lips don't quite meet?

steps.note: In bebé [beˈβe] you hear both: hard at the start of the word, soft in the middle.

steps.html: A preview of the full rule in lesson 10: hard [b] after a pause and after m or n; soft [β] everywhere else. So a word on its own like vino starts with a hard [b], with no v sound.

steps.html:
[ð] is the sound of English "th" in "the", "this" and "other". Spanish d has a soft version that is very close to it, between vowels and in most other positions: nada is [ˈnaða].

The Spanish version is lighter than English th: the tongue tip barely touches the edge of the teeth, with less friction.

Watch out for one trap: American English pronounces the d in "ladder" as a quick tap, [ɾ]. That tap is a Spanish r! If you say lado with an American "ladder" d, a Spanish speaker may hear laro.

steps.html:
Soft g, [ɣ] (the Greek letter gamma), follows the same pattern as [β] and [ð]. The back of the tongue rises toward the soft palate as if for g, but doesn't close. Air flows through with a soft, voiced friction.

English has nothing like it, so it takes practice. It's the voiced partner of the jota (lesson 15), and much gentler: almost a gargle with no effort behind it.

Say "aga" with a normal English g, and notice the back of your tongue sealing against the roof of your mouth. Now do it again but don't let it seal. Keep the voice on and let air slide through: "a-ɣa".
steps.yes: That's [ɣ]. Notice how much smoother lago sounds than "lah-go".
steps.no: Try saying "aga" while yawning slightly: the looser tongue tends to produce [ɣ] on its own. Or start from a gentle "a-ha" and add voice.

steps.html:
Hard [b d ɡ] appears:
  • after a pause, at the start of a phrase
  • after m or n
  • for d only, also after l
Soft [β ð ɣ] appears everywhere else, including across word boundaries. So dedo alone starts hard, but mi dedo starts soft. Spelling doesn't matter: b and v follow the same rule.

After m or n, your mouth is already closed (m) or the tongue is already sealed (n), so the next b, d or g comes out as a full stop: un dedo [un ˈd̪eðo]. After l, the tongue tip is already touching behind the teeth, which keeps d hard (caldo), but the lips and the back of the tongue are free, so b and g go soft (algo). After r, all three are soft (gordo, verdad).

steps.html: Before p, b, v or m, n becomes [m] (un poco [um ˈpoko]). Before k, g or j it becomes [ŋ], as in English "sing" (tengo, cinco). English does this too, so it comes naturally once you allow it.

steps.h: The r you already know how to make
steps.html:
A single Spanish r between vowels is a tap: one very quick flick of the tongue tip against the gum ridge. IPA writes it [ɾ], which looks like an r with its top cut off.

Good news: Americans already make this sound every day. The tt in "butter", the dd in "ladder" and the t in "water" are all taps: "butter" is [ˈbʌɾɚ].

It has nothing to do with the English r of "red", which IPA writes [ɹ]: there the tongue bunches or curls back and never touches anything.
Listen to the middle consonant in each English word. That quick flick is the same as Spanish r.
Say "butter" fast, American-style, and notice the tongue flick in the middle. Now say "bu-ɾa", then swap in Spanish words: pe-ɾo, pa-ɾa, ca-ɾo. Keep it light: a single touch, no English r colour.
steps.yes: That flick is [ɾ]. It's the most common r in Spanish.
steps.no: Say "a lot of" fast: "a-lo-ɾa". Or "got a": "go-ɾa". The middle is a tap. Then replace the first vowel: "pa-ɾa".
steps.q: Could you feel the single tongue flick?

steps.note: After a consonant (gracias, tres) and at the end of a word (comer) the r is also a tap. Don't let comer end with an English r.

steps.html:
The trill is the famous rolled r: the tongue tip rests loosely near the gum ridge and the air stream makes it flap several times in a row. IPA writes it with a plain [r].

That's confusing for English speakers: in IPA, [r] never means the English r (which is [ɹ]). Remember: [ɾ] = one tap, [r] = trill.

The difference changes meaning: pero [ˈpeɾo] "but" vs perro [ˈpero] "dog".

The trill is a matter of relaxation and air, not force:
  1. Say "butter-butter-butter" fast, then just the taps: "ɾ-ɾ-ɾ".
  2. Keep the tongue tip loose, right behind the teeth, and blow a strong stream of air past it.
  3. Another route: say "drrr" with the tongue forward, as in "dream", and let it run on.
Many adults need a few weeks of a minute a day. That's normal.
steps.yes: Great. Keep it short in words: 2 or 3 flaps is enough.
steps.no: Totally normal at first. Use a strong, slightly longer tap for now: it's far better than an English r, and everyone will understand you. Keep practising a minute a day.
steps.q: Did you get any vibration at all?

  • A single r after n, l or s is also the trill: Enrique, alrededor, Israel.
  • Every other single r is the tap [ɾ]: pero, caro, gracias.

steps.html:
In most of Latin America, y and ll are the same sound: [ʝ], a j with a curly tail. It's like English y in "yes" but with the tongue pressed a little closer to the palate, so there's a light buzz of friction.

Keep the two symbols apart: [j] is the plain English y glide (it appears in Spanish too, as in tierra [ˈt̪jera]). [ʝ] is the stronger consonant at the start of yo or in calle. After n or l, or when stressed, it can go further, toward the j of "jam".
The Spanish one has more contact and a slight buzz.

steps.html:
The jota, [x], is made where you make k: the back of the tongue rises toward the soft palate. But instead of closing, it leaves a narrow gap, and the air scrapes through. It's the sound of Scottish "loch" or German "Bach".

English h is different: it's just breath, with nothing in the mouth getting in the way. Spanish [x] has real friction.

And don't read the symbol as English x: IPA [x] is never "ks".

title: Words and sentences
sub: Stress, glides, linking, clusters, intonation and spelling: putting sounds together into real speech.

steps.html:
Spanish spelling tells you the stress every time:

  3. A written accent overrides both rules (ÁR-bol, ca-FÉ, can-CIÓN, te-LÉ-fo-no).

steps.html: Spanish speakers don't pause between words. A final consonant joins the next word's vowel (los otros is said lo-so-tros), and vowels at a word boundary blend (una amiga is u-na-mi-ga). IPA can mark this with a tie, ‿. This is why fast Spanish sounds like one long word.

steps.html:
Spanish sentence melody is close to English:
  • Statements fall at the end: Es tu casa. "It's your house."
  • Yes/no questions rise at the end, and that rise is often the only thing that makes them questions: ¿Hablas español?

Written Spanish warns you a question is coming with an upside-down ¿ at the start.

title: Tones and the IPA
sub: How IPA writes Mandarin, and the four tones: the one thing every Mandarin word has that English words don't.

steps.html:
Pinyin is the official way to write Mandarin in Latin letters. It's consistent, but it was designed for Chinese readers, so many letters don't mean what an English speaker expects: q in qī (seven) is nothing like English q, x in xī (west) isn't "ks", and c in cài (dish) is "ts" with a puff.

IPA shows what is actually said. Square brackets mean "pronounced like this": 七 qī is [tɕʰi˥]. Throughout this course you'll see pinyin and IPA side by side, so you learn to read both.

Every Mandarin syllable has three parts:
  1. an initial consonant (optional): the m of mā
  2. a final: a vowel, possibly with a glide before it or -n / -ng after it: the a of mā, the iang of jiāng
  3. a tone: the pitch shape over the whole syllable.
There are only about 400 initial + final combinations. Tones multiply them, and they're as much part of the word as the consonants: mā "mom" and mà "scold" are as different as "cat" and "bat".

lessons.title: b, d, g vs p, t, k: the puff

steps.html:
In English, b/p, d/t and g/k differ mainly in voicing (buzz). Mandarin doesn't use voicing at all. Instead, the pairs differ in aspiration, the puff of air:
  • pinyin b d g = [p t k]: no voice and no puff. Exactly the p of "spin", the t of "stop", the k of "skin".
  • pinyin p t k = [pʰ tʰ kʰ]: a strong puff, stronger than in English.
So 爸 bà is [pa˥˩], not an English b. If you voice it, people will still understand; if you skip the puff on p, t, k, they may hear the wrong word.

title: Tones in real speech
sub: Tone pairs, the tone-change rules, and whole phrases.

steps.html:
Most Mandarin words have two syllables, and tones sound different in combination than alone. Practising all 16 pairs is the fastest route to tones that sound natural.

Two tips: tone 3 is mostly just low, and it only rises at the end of a phrase. And tone 1 stays high, so don't let it sag before the next syllable.

steps.h: Two third tones in a row
steps.html: When two third tones meet, the first becomes a second tone: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo. Pinyin keeps writing the original tone, so you have to apply this yourself.
Before tones 1, 2 or 4 (or a neutral tone), a third tone only dips low and stays low (21). It doesn't rise. This low version is actually the most common form of tone 3.
Group the words by meaning and apply the rule inside each group: 我 / 很好 → wǒ hén hǎo. In fast speech you'll also hear wó hén hǎo.

steps.h: Tones don't go away in sentences
steps.html:
In English, pitch carries emotion and questions. In Mandarin, pitch is mostly busy carrying tones, so:
  • Questions are made with words, not pitch. 吗 ma at the end turns a statement into a yes/no question, and it's said in a light neutral tone. Don't let your voice swoop up on it like English.
  • Emotion changes the overall range (higher, wider, faster), but the tone shapes stay.
  • In a sentence, tones are smaller and quicker than in single words. Keep tone 1 high, and keep tone 3 low.
Every syllable gets its own beat, except neutral-tone syllables, which are short and light. Listen to the phrases below, then shadow them: play, and speak along with the recording at the same time.

steps.h: Three ways to write a word
steps.html:
You'll meet Arabic words in three forms:
  1. Arabic script, the real spelling (see the Read Arabic page). It usually leaves out short vowels.
  2. Transliteration into Latin letters, like ḥabībi or ʿēn. Every book uses a different system.
  3. IPA, which shows exactly what's said: حبيبي is [ħabiːbi].
This course teaches Levantine Arabic, the spoken Arabic of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. It differs from Modern Standard Arabic (the written language) in some sounds, and you'll learn both forms where they differ.

steps.h: Where ē and ō come from
steps.html:
Standard Arabic has two diphthongs, [aj] and [aw]. In Levantine they have become long, steady vowels:
  • [aj] → [eː]: bayt → بيت bēt "house", ʿayn → عين ʿēn "eye"
  • [aw] → [oː]: yawm → يوم yōm "day", tawb → توب tōb "garment"
The script writes them with ي and و, the same letters used for [iː] and [uː]. Nothing in normal spelling tells you which one a word has: تين is tīn but بيت is bēt. You learn it with each word, by ear.
English "say" and "no" glide toward another vowel. Levantine ē and ō hold one position from start to finish, like Spanish e and o, only longer.

Say bēt and hold the vowel for two full seconds: "beeeeet" with the "e" of "bed" made long. Watch your jaw in a mirror: it shouldn't rise at the end. Then do yōm, keeping your lips in the same rounded shape until the m.
steps.yes: That's it: long, steady vowels.
steps.no: Exaggerate the length first, then make sure nothing moves. If your jaw closes at the end, you're saying the English "ay".
steps.q: Could you keep the vowel steady?

steps.html:
Arabic a changes colour depending on its neighbours:
  • Bright, close to the a of "cat": next to most consonants. باب, جمال, كتب.
  • Dark, close to the a of "father": next to the emphatics ص ض ط ظ, and usually ق, خ, غ and ر. صار, طيب, راس.
Transcriptions (including this app) write both as [a] because the colour is predictable. Letting the consonant colour the vowel is a big part of sounding natural.

Many nouns and adjectives end in ة (tāʾ marbūṭa). Levantine says it as [e] after most consonants: مدرسة madrase, كبيرة kbīre, قهوة ʾahwe. But after the "back" consonants (emphatics, ح ع خ غ, ق) and usually after ر, it stays [a]: بيضة bēḍa, منيحة mnīḥa, ساعة sāʿa, شجرة shajara.

It's the same rule as the colour of a: back consonants pull the vowel back. (Lebanese speakers raise it even further, toward [i].)

lessons.title: The glottal stop, and Levantine ق

steps.html:
[ʔ] is the catch in "uh-oh": the vocal folds close and release. In Arabic it's a full consonant, written with hamza (ء أ إ).

And in Levantine, most ق letters are also said [ʔ]: قلب "heart" is ʾalb, هلق "now" is hallaʾ. The deep Standard [q], made with the back of the tongue against the uvula, survives in formal and religious words like قرآن.

Say "uh-oh" and freeze in the middle: you can feel your throat close. That closure is [ʔ]. Now say قلب as ʔalb, starting with that catch. For [q], say "k" but much further back, so the back of your tongue touches your uvula.
steps.yes: Good. In Levantine you'll mostly use the catch.
steps.no: Cough very gently: the start of a cough is a glottal stop.

steps.html:
ق is pronounced differently depending on who's talking and what they're saying:
  • City Levantine (Damascus, Beirut, Jerusalem, Amman): [ʔ], the glottal stop. قال ʾāl "he said", قهوة ʾahwe "coffee".

title: The emphatic consonants
sub: Four consonants made with the tongue root pulled back, and how they colour everything around them.

steps.h: A second, darker s and t
steps.html:
Arabic has "emphatic" versions of s, t, d and z. You make the normal consonant while pulling the root of your tongue back toward your throat (and lowering the middle of the tongue). IPA marks this with ˤ: ص [sˤ], ط [tˤ].

The consonant itself only changes a little. The bigger clue is the vowels next to it: they become deeper and darker. سار sār has a bright a, near "cat"; صار ṣār has a deep a, near "father".

Say "sss". Now, while still hissing, pull your tongue back and down as if you were about to say a deep "aw" (or as if someone pressed on your tongue with a spoon). The hiss gets lower and duller: [sˤ]. Add a deep a: ṣār. Compare with a bright sār.
steps.yes: The difference is in the whole syllable, not just the s.
steps.no: Say "sad" and "sod" in English: the vowel in "sod" is close to the vowel after an emphatic. Then make the s match the dark vowel.

lessons.title: ث ذ ظ: the Standard th sounds

steps.html:
Standard Arabic has three "th" sounds: ث [θ] as in "think", ذ [ð] as in "this", and ظ [ðˤ], an emphatic version of ð.

Levantine replaced them in two ways:
  • Everyday words: [t] [d] [dˤ]. تلاتة tlāte "three", دهب dahab "gold", ضهر ḍahr "back".
  • Words borrowed from Standard Arabic: [s] [z] [zˤ]. ثقافة saʾāfe "culture", ذكي zaki "smart", ظريف ẓarīf "nice".
You'll hear the original th sounds in the news, in formal speech and in the Quran, so it's worth knowing all three versions.

lessons.title: Rule: the article il- and sun letters

steps.h: il-, and when the l disappears
steps.html:
Levantine "the" is il- (or l- before a vowel or a consonant cluster). Before letters made with the tongue tip, called sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن, and in Levantine often ج), the l merges into the next consonant, which doubles: الشمس is iš-šams, not "il-shams". Before the other letters, the moon letters, the l stays: الباب il-bāb.

Spelling always shows ال, so you have to apply this yourself.

steps.html:
Levantine stress is predictable from the shape of the word. Check from the end:
  1. If the last syllable has a long vowel plus a consonant, or ends in two consonants, stress it: جميل ja-MĪL, كتاب KTĀB, مشغول mash-GHŪL.

  3. Otherwise, stress the third-to-last: مدرسة MAD-ra-se, مرحبا MAR-ḥa-ba, مكتبة MAK-ta-be.
English speakers tend to stress the wrong long vowel. Long vowels attract stress, but only in the positions above.

Books, news and signs use Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). People in Damascus, Beirut, Amman and Jerusalem speak Levantine, which changes some sounds in regular ways:

  • ذ [ð] → [d] (or [z])
  • ظ [ðˤ] → [zˤ] or [dˤ]
  • ج [dʒ] → [ʒ] in Syria and Lebanon

Unlike Mandarin, Levantine (like English) can turn a statement into a yes/no question just with rising intonation: إنت تعبان. "You're tired." vs إنت تعبان؟ "Are you tired?"

Question-word questions (شو "what", وين "where", كيف "how") usually fall at the end, as in English.
Many greetings have a fixed reply. صباح الخير "morning of goodness" is answered with صباح النور "morning of light". Shadow these until they come out smoothly: play, and speak along at the same time.
